newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Yachting - Peter Campbell's Rhumbline Column.
newsitem.headline: Australian Yachting - Peter Campbell's Rhumbline Column.

text.p: By Peter Campbell*
OLYMPIC YACHTING PLAN REVEALED

The controversial plan for the Olympic yachting site at Rushcutters Bay will be released either today or early next week, confirming that the old Navy site and adjacent parkland will be shore base headquarters for the Sydney 2000 Olympic sailing, over-riding the strong objections of some local residents.

The plan will allow for the demolition of some of the buildings now being used by the Navy s sail training centre which, incidentally, is now being wound down under Defence Forces budget cuts. However, the heritage buildings will be retained as headquarters for the Olympic sailing in Sydney 2000 - and for the Pre-Olympic Regattas in 1998 and 1999.
More significantly, following the Games, the site is expected to become the Australian Yachting Federation's administrative headquarters, but also including a national sailing centre.

During the Olympics, a number of temporary buildings or large marquees will be erected and adjacent Yarranabbe Park will be used as the boat park. Along the foreshore a temporary floating marina will be installed for up to 180 Olympic regatta support craft.

The yachting regatta in 2000 will not be quite as large as first predicted with the International Olympic Committee reducing the number of athletes in all sports. Yachting participants will be reduced from 443 at Savannah (Atlanta) to 400 in Sydney. However, for the two Pre-Olympic Regattas, each nation will be allowed two entries in each of the ten classes.

The Olympic racing will be sailed on two offshore and four onshore courses, with the match-racing finals for the Soling keelboats to be sailed in Farm Cove allowing the best spectator viewing in the history of Olympic sailing.
STRONG ENTRIES FOR WINTER RACING

There will be plenty of activity around Rushcutters Bay through the rest of autumn and winter months, with the Cruising Yacht Club of Australia already receiving more than 100 block entries for its popular Winter Series on Sydney Harbour. Club sailing director PHIL THOMPSON predicts the regular Sunday fleet could reach 150 boats during the winter.

The Series opens this Sunday with the ladies day race for the Jill McLeay Trophy, with the pointscore opening Sunday week. Most of Sydney s best ocean racing yachts have already entered for this highly competitive series, including watch-maker WARWICK MILLER's with his Hong Kong-registered Exile, solicitor MARTIN JAMES Infinity III and computer services executive GEOFF ROSS Yendys.

MILLER, who established his Guess Watches business in Hong Kong, has presented the CYCA with Guess watches as prizes for the top three placegetters in each division each Sunday of the Winter Series - quite a substantial donation back to the sport.
GLENN BOURKE FOR ADMIRAL'S CUP

Olympic sailing competition manager and former Olympic, World champion, America's Cup and Admiral's Cup sailor GLENN BOURKE has had to limit his sailing activities since taking on the job with SOCOG last September. He plans to get back to international sailing overseas this Northern Hemisphere summer, including the Admiral's Cup in England.
BOURKE will not be sailing for Australia. Instead he has signed up with the Italians who are defending the Admiral's Cup they won for the first time at Cowes in 1995.

BOURKE will be sailing as tactician aboard Brava Q8 in four regattas including the Admiral's Cup, a role performed by former America's Cup skipper Paul Cayard in 1995 who is currently involved in a Whitbread campaign. Skipper of Brava Q8 will be Italian former Star class world champion Enrico Chieffi.
NEW ZEALAND IN AMERICA'S CUP FORM
RUSSELL COUTTS and his Team New Zealand crew saved their best until last in winning the final 1997 Road to the Cup 2000 regattas in New Zealand on Waitamata Harbour off Auckland last weekend.

IN 15-20 knot winds, COUTTS and his crew produced the classic match race start to lock Englishman CHRIS LAW out of the start in what proved to be the fifth and last race of the contest. The Kiwis then clamped the classic cover on the Royal Dorset Yacht Club crew to win the series 4-1.

The Road to the Cup regattas have been sailed in New Zealand s two identical International America s Cup Class yachts from the 1992 America's with three regattas over the past few weeks in Wellington and Auckland. Team New Zealand, skippered by COUTTS, won 4-0 against the New York Yacht Club, skippered by ED BAIRD, in Wellington and then beat New York and BAIRD again in Auckland, this time 4-3, with Team New Zealand s alternative skipper MURRAY JONES in charge.

Meanwhile, there is no further word about Australian challengers for the Auld Mug with potential syndicates remaining tight-lipped about their plans. But we will be there, with a challenge through the Royal Sydney Yacht Squadron.
HISTORIC TRANS-ATLANTIC RECORD BROKEN

After 92 years, the Trans-Atlantic record set by the American schooner Atlantic in 1905, was broken this week by the Swedish-owned racing yacht Nicorette, skippered by LUDDE INGVALL, with a crew that included Australian ADRIENNE CAHALAN.

Nicorette, an 80-footer originally built for the aborted Grand Mistral Round-the-World Challenge, left Sandy Hook, New Jersey, on Tuesday, March 25 at 7:35:29 EST and crossed Lizard Point, Cornwall, at 1:57:58 GMT last Sunday, April 6.
Atlantic's record for the 3005 nautical miles stood at 12 days 4 hours 1 minute and Nicorette cut 14 hours 38 minutes 50 seconds off that time.
During the voyage, Nicorette negotiated icebergs and growlers and narrowly missed a whale spotted 10 metres from her bow.
- - - - BT GLOBAL CHALLENGE FLEET LEADER REACHES CAPE TOWN

Overall race leader, Group 4, has won the fourth leg of the BT Global Challenge, sailing the rugged 6,300 nautical mile course from Sydney to Cape Town in 39 days 11 hours 35 minutes 5 seconds. The fleet sailed from Sydney on March 2 with Group 4 reaching Cape Town last Wednesday, April 9.

Skippered by MIKE GOLDING, Group 4 had to battle to the bitter end to secure her victory, not taking the lead until the fleet had been ten days at sea. GOLDING told how the yacht encountered a storm with 55 knot winds and 60-foot waves on Good Friday.
Six Australians are involved in the Sydney to Cape Town leg. The first to finish was MARGOT DOUGLAS on board Commercial Union which, at last report, was expected to be fourth boat to finish.
* Peter Campbell is editor of OFFSHORE Yachting magazine.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800.
